claim: The pace limiter a game needs follows its structure: none where it waits on its own interrupts or HALTs, a fixed-stretch credit with no frame sync, a K window for a flat-out game.

evidence.text: A game that waits on its own interrupts needs no K window on its update; 28 MHz to the wait is enough. Fine K windows on every tile only added cost.
evidence.quote: A game that waits on its own interrupts needs no K window on its update; 28 MHz to the wait is enough.

evidence.text: Plots run at 28 MHz and pay for the overlay; the HALTs hold the pace: an update has a frame of slack, more than one frame's work takes three. No pace window.
evidence.quote: The HALTs hold the pace: an update has a frame of slack, more than one frame's work takes three. No pace window.

evidence.text: A game with no frame sync and a hook cost per draw needs no limiter: run a fixed stretch of the same draw's own set-up at 28 MHz; the credit scales with the draws and no wait is added.
evidence.quote: A game with no frame sync and a hook cost per draw needs no limiter: run a fixed stretch of the same draw's own set-up at 28 MHz.

evidence.text: A game with no frame wait needs a K window round all it can, or every hook entry at 3.5 MHz is its own cost.
evidence.quote: A game with no frame wait needs a K window round all it can, or every hook entry at 3.5 MHz is its own cost.

evidence.text: A CPU-bound game whose hooks cost more than the original's idle time: run one of its own long routines (the renderer, 38 ms) at 28 MHz in a game-routine window; +15% -> within 1%.
